title: Arlen's Urgent Delivery
markdown:
Once upon a time, high in the Skyshard Mountains, lived an elf named Arlen. His days were spent tending his garden, where the luminous moonpetal flowers glowed like captured moonlight. Arlen was a mountain elf, wise in the ways of the wind and sun, but sometimes a gust of forgetfulness would blow through his mind, and he’d forget to check the weather. This often led to a soggy patch of chives drooping sadly, their tiny leaves waterlogged.

Every day, Arlen sketched the jagged mountain peaks against the blue sky, his charcoal flying across the parchment. He hummed a low, rumbling tune, as ancient as the mountains themselves, while he watered his prize moonpetal flowers. Their velvety petals unfurled slowly, revealing centers that glowed with a soft, pearly light. Arlen found their inner glow completely captivating.

One day, the usual quiet of his cliffside home was broken by a flurry of activity. A small, chirping messenger bird, its feathers ruffled and legs trembling, landed on his windowsill with a soft thud. It carried a rolled-up scroll tied with a shimmering silver ribbon. Arlen’s sharp elf eyes quickly read the hurried script. The message stated that a special parcel he was guarding for the elder of the Whispering Falls was now incredibly important and must be delivered before the moon reached its highest point. A sliver of moon was already visible in the sky, and the Whispering Falls were a half-day's climb away. His heart gave a nervous flutter.

Arlen snatched up the parcel, a small, carved wooden box that felt surprisingly light but held great importance. He dashed out his door, the scent of pine needles and damp earth filling his lungs. He hadn't gone twenty steps before a booming voice echoed from a nearby bell tower. "Arlen, my nimble friend! Have you heard about the moss? The kind that grows on north-facing rocks has a peculiar shimmer, like tiny emeralds sprinkled with stardust!” It was Barnaby, the goblin bell-ringer. Barnaby loved collecting oddities, especially shiny things or interesting fungi, and he loved sharing his discoveries even more. He launched into a dizzying tale of his moss-finding adventure, complete with dramatic gestures and much bell-jingling.

Arlen’s stomach did a flip-flop. The sun was dipping lower, painting the sky in oranges and purples, casting long shadows across the valleys. He mumbled a hasty apology about the urgent delivery, his voice tight with a new kind of worry. He scrambled towards the rope bridges that crossed the dizzying chasms between the peaks. The wind tugged at his tunic as he hurried across a swaying span, the dense pine forests a blur of green far below. The creaking ropes and whistling wind made him feel very small and alone. Suddenly, a vast shadow fell over him, blotting out the fading sunlight. He looked up, shielding his eyes, to see a magnificent dragon, its scales the color of polished bronze, hovering gently.

“Greetings, young elf!” boomed a voice that rumbled like distant thunder, yet was surprisingly gentle. “It appears you are in a hurry. Could I give you a lift? Perhaps a strong updraft from my left wing to hasten your journey? It’s quite efficient, if I do say so myself.” The dragon, Sir Reginald Scorchwing, puffed out his chest proudly.

Arlen, awestruck by the dragon’s magnificence, shook his head, trying to keep his voice steady. “Thank you, Sir Reginald, your offer is kind, but I must be swift. The elder awaits! And, with all due respect, Sir Reginald, your wing-wind might send me flying towards the Frozen Peaks, and that’s not quite the direction of the Whispering Falls.” A prickle of anxiety tightened in his chest. The dragon’s help was well-intentioned, but his understanding of wind currents seemed as flamboyant as his flight.

Arlen’s worry grew into an urgent concern. He was losing precious time, and the moon was now a pale sliver climbing higher in the darkening sky. He remembered a secret, overgrown path, a shortcut known only to the oldest mountain dwellers, a path whispered about by his grandmother. He ducked off the main trail, pushing through tangled brambles that snagged his clothes and scratched his arms. Just as he thought he was making good progress, a grumpy, whiskered face popped out from behind a moss-covered rock. A marmot, its fur the color of damp earth and its eyes like tiny, glittering obsidian beads, puffed its chest out indignantly. "Oi! You can't just stomp through here! This path is mine!" it squeaked, its voice surprisingly loud. Arlen paused, observing the creature carefully. The marmot was busy polishing a smooth, grey stone with a bit of bright green lichen, its little paws working with great concentration. Arlen recalled that Barnaby the goblin sometimes gifted shiny pebbles to local marmots to keep them in a good mood.

Finally, with the moon now a brilliant pearl high in the inky sky, Arlen burst through the last of the undergrowth and found himself at the edge of the Whispering Falls. The air was thick with the scent of damp earth, moss, and sweet pine needles. The distant roar of the waterfall whispered secrets, and the cool, polished surface of the silver bell felt reassuring in his trembling hand. He needed to get the elder's attention now, before the moon reached its absolute highest point. He remembered Barnaby's bells, how some tones carried further than others. Arlen reached into his satchel and pulled out a small, silver bell he’d found weeks ago on a high ridge, captivated by its bright, clear ring. He held it aloft, its polished surface catching the moonlight, and gave it a sharp, clear ring. The sound was pure and high, a perfect echo of Barnaby’s bells.

A moment later, a wizened face with kind, ancient eyes peered out from a hidden cave mouth behind the shimmering curtain of the waterfall. The elder, a stooped figure draped in moss-green robes, beckoned him forward. Arlen, his breath coming in ragged gasps, stumbled forward and presented the parcel, his hands still trembling slightly. The elder accepted it with a knowing nod, a faint smile on his lips. "You have done well, mountain-bred elf," the elder said, his voice like the rustling of dry leaves. "Your quick thinking and your keen ears have saved the day. The echoes of that bell are a rare and welcome sound." Arlen felt a warmth spread through him, a satisfaction far greater than any prize-winning moonpetal, a feeling of true accomplishment.

Ever since then, Arlen still tended his garden with diligence, but he always checked the weather, making a little diagram on his doorpost to remind himself. And sometimes, when the wind carried the faint echo of bells, he would smile, remembering his unexpected journey and the little silver bell that had found its true purpose. He also discovered that Barnaby the goblin bell-ringer was quite happy to trade chimes for a well-polished smooth stone, especially if it had a nice shimmer. Arlen now had a small, carefully arranged collection on his windowsill, each one a reminder of a time when a very important parcel, a polite dragon, and a grumpy marmot all led him to discover something new about himself, and the surprising usefulness of a well-placed chime.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for older children
